Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1214/aop/1024404523, fetched) title 'When is the Student $t$-statistic asymptotically standard normal?', authors Evarist Gine, Friedrich Götze, David M. Mason, pages 1514-1531, print 1997-07-01. Crossref abstract (verbatim, saved /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify32h-L07-L08/cr/crossref_abstracts.json): 'Let X, X_i, i in N, be independent, identically distributed random variables. It is shown that the Student t-statistic based upon the sample {X_i} is asymptotically N(0,1) if and only if X is in the domain of attraction of the normal law.' Scope check: the abstract states no mean-zero condition. A later restatement by Mason and Shao (2001), Annals of Probability 29(4) 1435-1450, doi 10.1214/aop/1015345757 (Crossref abstract, read): 'Giné, Götze and Mason (1997) proved that T_n converges in distribution to a standard normal random variable if and only if X is in the domain of attraction of a normal random variable and EX = 0.' So the GGM result carries EX = 0. The span does not state it, but both places it appears follow an explicit zero-Sharpe-ratio sentence in the same paragraph (Remark 2.9: 'If SR = 0 and the variance is finite ...'; section 7: 'At a zero Sharpe ratio the statistic is a Student t-statistic, which ...'), so the mean-zero condition is supplied in context. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L08.html section 5 (line 272): containment, monotone expected maximum, and the null-win statement
rows.evidence: unchanged since 1e380ee (git diff checked); round-18 evidence: Re-derived. Let Q_N be the maximum of N null statistics and X_N the new null. Q_N = max(Q_(N-1), X_N) >= Q_(N-1) pointwise, for any joint law of the statistics. (a) E[Q_N] >= E[Q_(N-1)]: the expected maximum cannot fall as N grows. (b) {Z + delta > Q_N} is a subset of {Z + delta > Q_(N-1)}, so the probability that the genuine configuration wins cannot rise (containment, the T span that was already at 584f614). (c) The complement: P(some null beats the genuine) = 1 - P(genuine wins) cannot fall, so 'the null configurations win at least as often' (T). Bound: Lesson 1 Theorem 2.1 (L01.html line 82) states 'Let Z_1, ..., Z_N each have the standard normal distribution, with any joint distribution, and N >= 2. Then E[max Z_n] <= sqrt(2 ln N)'; its proof (Jensen, e^(lambda E M) <= sum E e^(lambda Z_n) = N e^(lambda^2/2), then lambda = sqrt(2 ln N)) is re-derived and holds with no independence. Numerical spot check (scratch scripts/l08_sec5_monotone.py, seed 777, 60,000 draws, N up to 60; output out_l08_sec5_monotone.txt): E[max] of the first N is non-decreasing in N for an equicorrelated law (rho 0.9), independent normals, a comonotone law and a block-random law; at every N it lies below sqrt(2 ln N) (smallest margins 0.9973, 0.5416, 1.1820 and 0.5990); P(genuine wins) with k nulls, k = 1..39, is non-increasing (0.8778, 0.8185, 0.7111, 0.6612, 0.5417, ... ). All checks pass. [round 19: course/modules/S/S7/L08.html, its labs, figures and cards are byte-identical at 1e380ee and f14987f (git diff; structure fingerprint identical).]

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L08.html section 5, T span (line 272): 'The luck, the expected maximum of the nulls, cannot fall as N grows, because adding a null can only raise the maximum; for standard normal null statistics with any joint law it is at most sqrt(2 ln N) (Lesson 1, Theorem 2.1)'
rows.evidence: unchanged since 1e380ee (git diff checked); round-18 evidence: Re-derived at d10fb51. Monotonicity: with N+1 nulls the maximum is the pointwise maximum over N nulls and one more variable, so it is at least the N-null maximum for every outcome, and its expectation cannot fall. Bound: for any joint law of Z_1..Z_N standard normal, e^{lambda E max Z_n} <= E e^{lambda max Z_n} (Jensen) <= sum_n E e^{lambda Z_n} = N e^{lambda^2/2}, so E max Z_n <= ln N / lambda + lambda/2 for every lambda > 0; lambda = sqrt(2 ln N) gives sqrt(2 ln N). The statement matches Lesson 1, Theorem 2.1 (L01.html line 82), whose scope is 'any joint distribution', and the L08 claim uses no wider scope. The index is the page's N (configurations), and the claim uses the N-1 nulls, with sqrt(2 ln(N-1)) <= sqrt(2 ln N). Concept link to L01 def-expected-maximum-sharpe exists (check_dag PASS). Card S7-c227 now covers it (L08-sec5-expected-max-card-gap). rows.evidence: unchanged since 1e380ee (git diff checked); round-18 evidence: Claim: adding a null trial cannot raise the probability that a genuine configuration wins in sample, whatever the joint law. Proof (re-derived): let X0 be the genuine in-sample statistic and M_k the maximum of k null statistics. The winning event with k nulls is {X0 > M_k}; adding a null Y gives {X0 > max(M_k, Y)}, which is contained in {X0 > M_k}, so its probability cannot exceed the earlier one. No independence or distributional assumption is used. Numerical spot check (scratch scripts/spot_checks.py, 400,000 draws, a common-factor joint law, N-1 = 0,1,4,9,39 nulls): the win probability is non-increasing at every size (for example 0.6448 -> 0.4817 when a second null is added, 0.0513 -> 0.0502 at 39 nulls). The card's back matches Section 5's text. Grade T is right (a proof on the page). PASS. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html Remark 2.9 (line 204): T span 'If SR = 0 and the variance is finite, sqrt(T) SR-hat = (sqrt(T) mu-hat/sigma)(sigma/sigma-hat) -> N(0,1), by the CLT for mu-hat, the LLN for sigma-hat and Slutsky's lemma'
rows.evidence: unchanged since 1e380ee (git diff checked); round-18 evidence: Derivation re-checked step by step. (i) SR-hat = mu-hat/sigma-hat, so sqrt(T) SR-hat = (sqrt(T) mu-hat/sigma)(sigma/sigma-hat) is an identity. (ii) With iid returns, mean mu = SR sigma = 0 and finite variance sigma^2, the CLT gives sqrt(T) mu-hat/sigma -> N(0,1). (iii) sigma-hat^2 = (1/(T-1)) sum (r - r-bar)^2 -> sigma^2 in probability by the LLN applied to r^2 (finite since E r^2 < infinity) and r-bar -> 0; so sigma/sigma-hat -> 1 in probability (the divisor T or T-1 does not matter). (iv) Slutsky gives the limit N(0,1). Nothing beyond finite variance is used. Numerical spot check (scratch num_checks.py, 20000 replications): Student t with 3 df scaled to unit variance, SR = 0: P(z <= -1.6449) = 0.0513 / 0.0502 / 0.0502 and P(z <= 1.6449) = 0.9505 / 0.9500 / 0.9506 at T = 250 / 1000 / 4000 (N(0,1): 0.05 and 0.95); sd(z) = 1.007 / 1.001 / 0.992. The fourth moment is infinite there, so the check is of the claim's sufficiency. Grade T is right (proved on the page). The iid standing assumption is the section 1 assumption ('keep independence'). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html Corollary 5.2 (line 405-410), Proposition 5.4 (line 425-431), key-results rows 747-748
rows.evidence: unchanged since 1e380ee (git diff checked); round-18 evidence: New row; re-derived and spot-checked numerically (scratch math_checks.py, output math_checks_out.txt). Influence of the Sharpe estimator for standardized return u: psi = u - (SR/2)(u^2 - 1); Var psi = 1 + SR^2/2; Cov(psi1, psi2) = rho + SR1 SR2 rho^2 / 2 (Isserlis: E[u1 u2] = rho, E[u1 u2^2] = 0, E[u1^2 u2^2] = 1 + 2 rho^2). Hence theta = Var(psi1 - psi2) = 2(1 - rho) + (SR1^2 + SR2^2)/2 - SR1 SR2 rho^2, the Corollary 5.2 formula (row 747). Monte Carlo with 4,000,000 draws for SR pairs (0.05,0.05), (0.1,0.3), (0.5,1.0) and rho in {-0.9,-0.5,0,0.5,0.9}: largest |MC - closed form| = 0.0035, consistent with MC error. Sign check (common SR in {0.05, 0.5, 1.3, 1.41}, rho in +-{0.1, 0.5, 0.99}): sign(theta - (V1+V2)) = -sign(rho) for every point. So Proposition 5.4's "undersized under positive correlation, oversized under negative" holds for SR^2 < 2. The limit (line 427) follows from Theorem 5.1, sqrt((T-1)/T) -> 1 and Slutsky's lemma, as the proof on lines 433-436 states; the proof's identity (V1+V2) - theta = rho(2 + SR^2 rho) (line 436) matches the derivation above. It reads: 'We propose a general framework to assess the probability of backtest overfitting (PBO) ... we call these implementations combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (CSCV). We show that CSCV produces reasonable estimates of PBO for several useful examples.' The 'Need to know' summary reads: 'Results indicate that CSCV provides reasonable estimates of PBO, with relatively small errors.' The span's claim is what the abstract shows: CSCV is introduced as one way to estimate PBO, and the reasonable estimates are for 'several useful examples' that are the authors' own test cases. (2) Raw-N hurdle in units of 1/sqrt(T): sqrt(0.5545) x bracket(100) = 0.744648 x 2.530603 = 1.884405 -> 1.884, where bracket(100) = (1-gamma) Phi^-1(0.99) + gamma Phi^-1(1 - 1/(100 e)) = 2.530603 (page 2.5306). (3) Within cluster k, sqrt(T) SR_n = sqrt(0.9) W_k + sqrt(0.1) eps_n (the decomposition has variance 0.9 + 0.1 = 1 and within-cluster correlation 0.9); the cluster maximum is Y_k = sqrt(0.9) W_k + sqrt(0.1) Q_k with Q_k the maximum of 50 standard normals: derivation checked. (4) E[Q_k] = 2.2490736 -> 2.249, Var[Q_k] = 0.2157124 -> 0.216 (scipy quad; see L07-num-problems). Y_k has mean sqrt(0.1) x 2.249 = 0.711196 -> 0.711 and sd sqrt(0.9 + 0.1 x 0.216) = sqrt(0.9216) = 0.960000 -> 0.960. (5) Two independent normals with these moments: E[max] = 0.711196 + 0.960/sqrt(pi) = 1.252818 -> 1.25. A Monte Carlo of the exact cluster model (seed 1, 400000 draws, scale check only, not on the page) gives 1.2518 (s.e. 0.0013), consistent with the approximation. (6) Overstatement: 1.884/1.2528 - 1 = 0.504 (0.507 with the unrounded hurdle 1.8845): 'about 50%' is right. The claim 'conservative for this structure' follows (hurdle above the truth). The 'no general sign' sentence is a remark. PASS. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html line 521 (Lab 4 interpretation, part 3): 'At T_beta the first-order mean of the statistic is sqrt(T_beta - 1) SR/sqrt(b(SR)) = sqrt(914) x 0.09/sqrt(1.1962) = 2.488'
rows.evidence: Derivation written out. Z_T = SR-hat sqrt(T-1)/sqrt(b-hat) is the statistic inside formula (2) (Remark 2.9). At the true moments its first-order mean is sqrt(T-1) SR/sqrt(b(SR)), with b(SR) = 1 - gamma3 SR + (gamma4 - 1)/4 SR^2; for the lab's mirrored exponential shock (gamma3 = -2, raw gamma4 = 9) b(SR) = 1 + 2 SR + 2 SR^2. At T_beta = 915: sqrt(914) x 0.09 / sqrt(1.1962) = 2.487790 (scratch l07_line521_check.out, line (A)), which rounds to the page's 2.488. Numerical spot-check (scratch l07_line521_check.py, section F): 400,000 replications of the lab's Part 3 data-generating process at n = 915 (independent seed 20261020; statistic formed from the sample moments as in the lab): mean(Z) = 2.4974 (s.e. 0.0015). The first-order value is 0.0096 lower, about 6.6 standard errors, the order-1/T finite-sample correction that the word 'first-order' covers. Result: PASS.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html line 521: 'sqrt(T_beta - 1)' with T_beta = 915 and 'sqrt(914)'; the T_beta (915 days) and MinTRL (401 days) of parts (3)
rows.evidence: T_beta = ceil(1 + b((z_0.95 + z_0.80)/SR)^2) = ceil(914.034) = 915 (scratch l07_line521_check.out, line (D)); the lab prints '80%_power 915'. T_beta - 1 = 914. MinTRL = ceil(1 + b(z_0.95/SR)^2) = ceil(400.552) = 401; the lab prints 'MinTRL 401'. (T_beta - 1)/(MinTRL - 1) = 2.285, which rounds to 2.29 (line (E)); key-results row 763 and Remark 2.9 print 2.29. The old value 2.486 is the mean at the unrounded T_beta, where it equals z_0.95 + z_0.80 = 2.486475; at the whole-day T_beta = 915 the mean is 2.488. Result: PASS.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html line 521: 'b(SR) = 1 + 2SR + 2SR^2', 'b(0.09)' bracket 1.1962, 'b'(SR)' and 'first-order standard deviation ... = 0.91' (sentence 3 of the interpretation) and '0.911' in the prediction
rows.evidence: b(0.09) = 1 + 2(0.09) + 2(0.09)^2 = 1.1962; b'(SR) = 2 + 4 SR = 2.36 (both on the page). First-order standard deviation of the statistic: 1 - SR b'(SR)/(2 b) = 1 - 0.2124/2.3924 = 0.911219, which rounds to 0.911 (the first sentence prints 0.91). Derivation: Var(SR-hat) is about b/(T-1), and d/dSR-hat [SR-hat/sqrt(b(SR-hat))] = (1/sqrt(b))(1 - SR-hat b'/(2b)), so Var(Z) is about (1 - SR b'/(2b))^2. Spot-check (scratch l07_line521_check.out, section F): the 400,000-replication sd(Z) = 0.9168 (s.e. about 0.0010), against 0.9112 at first order. The claim that the plug-in standard error rises with SR-hat and so narrows the spread is consistent: b increases in SR-hat because gamma3 < 0, and the sd is below 1. Result: PASS.
